title: Example theory: linear algebra
description:
A first look at vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$: the standard basis, adding two arrows with the parallelogram rule, and stretching (or flipping) a vector by a scalar. Drag the components and the scalar in the cards; orbit the view to see depth.

## Standard basis

The **standard basis** of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the triple of unit arrows along the coordinate axes:

$$\hat{\imath}=(1,0,0),\quad \hat{\jmath}=(0,1,0),\quad \hat{k}=(0,0,1).$$

Any vector is a **linear combination** of these directions — its coordinates *are* the coefficients:

$$\mathbf{u}=u_x\hat{\imath}+u_y\hat{\jmath}+u_z\hat{k}=(u_x,u_y,u_z).$$

## Vector addition

Addition is **componentwise**, which is the same as the geometric **parallelogram** (or tip-to-tail) rule:

$$\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}=(u_x+v_x,\,u_y+v_y,\,u_z+v_z).$$

Place $\mathbf{v}$ at the tip of $\mathbf{u}$ (dashed edge): that tip is $\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}$. The other dashed edge is $\mathbf{u}$ placed at the tip of $\mathbf{v}$. Both paths meet at the same point — addition is commutative.

## Scalar multiplication

A real number $c$ **stretches** $\mathbf{u}$ along the same line:

$$c\mathbf{u}=(c u_x,\,c u_y,\,c u_z).$$

- $|c|>1$ lengthens; $0<|c|<1$ shortens; $c=0$ collapses to the origin.
- $c<0$ **reverses** direction (a $180^\circ$ flip) and then stretches by $|c|$.
- $c\mathbf{u}$ is always **parallel** to $\mathbf{u}$ (or zero).

Length scales by the absolute value: $\|c\mathbf{u}\|=|c|\,\|\mathbf{u}\|$.

Together, addition and scalar stretch are the two operations that make $\mathbb{R}^3$ a **vector space** — every later idea in the course (span, linear maps, matrices) is built from these.
